ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: worship of the gods
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: How the colony keeps its gods: places given to them and the offerings left there, prayers in hard moments, the gods' festivals, vows, a priest, the gods in dreams, and faith that holds or breaks.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Select an altar, an ideogram, a sculpture or a nature shrine and press "Dedicate to a god": once someone has said the words there, it is that god's place, and offerings and prayers go to it.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: The gods are worshipped the way people have always worshipped: at a place set apart, with gifts, prayers, feast days and promises. In the colony's age a dedicated place is a shrine, a chapel, a church or a terminal. How it all plays out depends on how real the gods are: in Believed nothing supernatural happens and the colony reads its gods into chance, in Felt the gods act but never so plainly that nobody could doubt it, and in Walking they act in plain sight. The colony's standing with a god is only ever in words.

points.li: Any altar or ritual place (Ideology's, Alpha Memes', Vanilla Ideology Expanded's), any work of art, Royalty's nature shrines and the archotechs' ancient terminals can be given to a god with the button on it. The priest goes to say the words, else someone who prays to that god, else anyone free; until then it waits, and after two days unsaid the request lapses.

Now and then someone carries an offering from the stores to a god's place: what that god likes (food for the harvest and the hearth, a hunt's best pelt, a weapon for war, silver for the road, machine parts for the machine, anything for the Hunger), something the colony can spare and worth a fair gift, never a fortune. It is set down beside the place and left forbidden.

What happens to it follows how real the gods are. Walking: the god takes it before everyone's eyes. Felt: it is gone by morning and nobody saw it go. Believed: an animal comes and eats it, someone passing takes it, or it spoils or goes back to the stores, and the colony says the god sent them.

A god is pleased by a gift's worth, by how well it suits the god, and by its nature: a proud god wants the best made, a generous one food shared, a playful one art and good cheer. Archotechs take no offerings at all: they judge deeds.

Colonists pray in hard moments: when they or someone close is gravely ill, when someone of the colony has died, when raiders come, and in a drought in the growing season. The devout pray most, the wavering little, scoffers never.
In their free time they walk to their god's place and kneel there, or kneel where they stand; the sick pray in bed, and with raiders at the gate a word is said where they are.

A prayer comforts: a little strain eased, and a small moment of hope. Sometimes the god answers at the strength of how real the gods are: a fever eases, the grieving dream of the one lost, a fighter is steadied, rain comes. A priest, a god's own place and the god honoured this year make an answer likelier. Never in Believed.

A prayer that comes good on its own (the sick get well, the rain comes, nobody falls) is credited to the god. One that goes unanswered can be a crisis of faith: a hard few days, and with Ideology their certainty shaken. Two in a month and they may turn to another god, often a rival of the one that failed them.
The Hunger answers anyone, and comes back the next night for its due: something of worth gone from the stores.

Each of the colony's gods (up to three: the one honoured this year, its patron, the most widely held) has a festival on the colony's calendar, on its domain's day as the seasons fall in this land: the harvest's thanksgiving late in the fall, the longest night at midwinter, the dead's day as the fall turns.

A festival comes round like any day on the calendar and is kept with a feast by default. Besides the feast, the priest keeps the god's rite at its place, with Alpha Memes' or Ideology's chant for the god's kind where those are loaded, an offering is carried there, and a people that holds the god may send a few of its own.
Kept, the god is pleased; let pass, it is displeased. Three years running, a festival becomes a tradition like any other day.

No meat until the sick recover: sometimes a prayer for someone close and gravely ill becomes this vow. The one who made it asks the council for vegetarian meals in the stores. Kept when the sick get well (or after twenty days), broken by a single meal with meat in it.

A pilgrimage and a temple are life goals for the devout: setting their heart on one is a vow. The pilgrim walks on a free day to the god's holy place on the colony's land (an old tree, the water's edge, the graves, the far edge of the land) and prays an hour there. A temple is a place of the god's indoors in a room of impressiveness 50 or more and 16 cells or more.
A beast spared: a hunter whose god's sacred animal walks the land may vow that the colony won't hunt its kind for a season.
A kept vow pleases the god and gives pride; a broken one displeases it and gives shame, and a god that takes a broken word hard may show its anger.

With the gods on and a god the colony holds, a priest's seat opens on the council (a shaman, a priest, a pastor or an oracle by the colony's age), by Social and faith; A RimWorld of Magic's priests, paladins and brightmages stand first. With Ideology and a faith of the colony's own, the chaplain is the colony's priest instead.
The priest dedicates places, carries offerings, leads the festivals' rites, and is heard more surely by the gods.

The council is asked which god the colony honours this year (its festival first, its prayers and rites count for more, and its rivals notice), whether to vow a temple, what to do when a god asks for the colony's finest beast or the rain stays away, and how to settle the colony's people when they pray to two rival gods.

li.heading: Dreams
li.text: Now and then a dream is a god's: a warning of something real (a beast sacred to it marked for the hunt, a sickness among the colony, its own anger), a demand for an offering at its place within three days, the name of a god the colony didn't know, or a vision of the gods' ties. The priest and anyone with a psychic gift dream of the gods more often and see them plainly. A demand met pleases the god; let go, it displeases.

points.li: Scoffers (whose faith despises religion or has no gods, or who are far from sure of theirs) mock what the believers saw, to their faces, and the believer is hurt by it and the god offended.
A couple who pray to different gods argue over whose god sent the rain when it comes after a dry spell.

With A RimWorld of Magic, a caster's mana comes back faster while the colony stands well with their god (the one their class serves, else the one they pray to), slower while it is displeased, and not at all while it is wrathful. Nothing in Believed.
